Pen Registers go way back in the history of telephony. It was a device which actually had an ink pen which marked a page of paper (or in some cases, a photoreactuve papaer roll like the old-school Thermofax machines). The device was physically connected to the telephone wires in the nearest telephone exchange switching center. Then when that target number called out, the electromechanical impulses of the stepping switch would activate the register, indicating and recording the number of pulses made.

--- Research the telephone exchange stepping Relay system developed in the 1920's, which made the electrical connection between a calling line and a receiving line. The Relay system was used to replace the actual operator sitting at the plug panel responding to you picking up the receiver or cranking the handle, then saying "number please". The digital exchange did away with all of that. The last "manual switching center" was shut down in the 1990's. You can see and hear one if you go to the Smithsonian -- it's in the "mechanical technology" building.

The name "Pen Register" is archaic, but used in legal requests because the US Code on communications interception still refers to that 1920's nomenclature.

Today, it is simple, since physical access to the switching center is not necessary. The agency presents the writ/subpoena authorization to the provider and the provider uses their internal system to add an "extension" to the targeted number. That extension is routed to the agency's monitoring facility whose equipment captures everything -- voice, data, etc which are both inward and/or outward-bound. Digital quality capture with not a single click, bleeps, hoops, crackles, etc., as seen on spy movies. It's a trivial exercise to set up and most (if not all) telecommunications providers have at least one individual in a secure room within the facility to work the problem.
